lesson.title: Four Conditions, One Powerful Model: Recognizing the Binomial Setting
lesson.summary: A chance process qualifies as a binomial setting only when it has a fixed number of trials, exactly two outcomes per trial, a constant probability of success, and independent trials, and checking all four conditions is the essential first step before using binomial formulas.
lesson.body:
Many of the most useful discrete random variables in statistics count the number of successes in a repeated chance process: the number of free throws made out of 10 attempts, the number of defective items in a batch, the number of heads in a series of coin flips. Not every repeated process qualifies for the powerful binomial formulas used later in the course, though. Before applying them, you must confirm the situation is a genuine binomial setting by checking four specific conditions.

First, a fixed number of trials: the process is repeated a set number of times, usually called n, decided in advance rather than depending on the outcomes themselves. Second, two outcomes: each individual trial results in exactly one of two outcomes, typically labeled success and failure. Third, a constant probability: the probability of success, usually called p, is the same on every single trial. Fourth, independent trials: the outcome of any one trial does not affect the probability of success on any other trial, connecting directly back to the idea of independent events covered earlier in the course.

Test all four conditions on a concrete example, and build the resulting distribution by hand. Flip a fair coin 3 times, and let X be the number of heads. There is a fixed number of trials, n = 3, decided before any flip occurs. Each flip has exactly two outcomes, heads or tails. The probability of heads is 0.5 on every flip, regardless of what happened on previous flips, so the probability is constant. And the result of one flip has zero effect on any other flip, so the trials are independent. All four conditions hold, so X is a binomial random variable.

Because X is also a discrete random variable, its full probability distribution can be built by listing all 8 equally likely outcomes of 3 coin flips and counting the heads in each: HHH has 3 heads, HHT, HTH, and THH each have 2 heads, HTT, THT, and TTH each have 1 head, and TTT has 0 heads. Since each of the 8 outcomes has probability 1/8, this gives P(X = 0) = 1/8 = 0.125, P(X = 1) = 3/8 = 0.375, P(X = 2) = 3/8 = 0.375, and P(X = 3) = 1/8 = 0.125. Checking validity, as in an earlier chapter: every probability is between 0 and 1, and 1/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 + 1/8 = 8/8 = 1, so the distribution is valid.

From this table, E(X) = 0(1/8) + 1(3/8) + 2(3/8) + 3(1/8) = 0 + 3/8 + 6/8 + 3/8 = 12/8 = 1.5. So on average you would expect 1.5 heads in 3 flips, which matches the simple intuition that 3 flips at a 50 percent chance each should average out to half of 3. Later in the course you will meet a shortcut, E(X) = n times p, that gives this same answer instantly, 3 times 0.5 equals 1.5, without needing to build the full distribution table, but it is worth having done it by hand once to see exactly where that shortcut comes from.

Now a counter example, to sharpen where the boundary actually falls. Suppose instead you draw 3 cards from a standard 52 card deck without replacement, and let Y be the number of aces drawn. This looks similar at first glance, a fixed number of trials and two outcomes per draw, ace or not. But it fails the last two conditions. Before any cards are drawn, 4 of the 52 cards are aces, but if the first card drawn happens to be an ace, only 3 of the remaining 51 cards are aces, so the probability of drawing an ace on the next draw has changed. That also means the draws are not independent, since the outcome of the first draw alters the odds for the second. Because the probability is not constant and the trials are not independent, Y is not a binomial random variable, even though it also counts successes across a fixed number of trials. If each card were instead replaced and the deck reshuffled before the next draw, the probability of an ace would reset to 4/52 every time, restoring both constant probability and independence, and the situation would then qualify as a binomial setting.

Recognizing a binomial setting is as much a checklist skill as a computational one. Before reaching for any binomial formula, pause and confirm all four conditions, fixed number of trials, two outcomes, constant probability, independent trials, actually hold in the specific situation described. Getting this identification right is what lets everything covered in this unit, discrete random variables, probability distributions, expected value, and variance, connect smoothly to the binomial distribution's own mean and variance formulas coming next in the course.
